crates.name: apsis-core
crates.summary: Shared foundation types for the ApsisRS workspace: a general purpose error type, result aliases, physical constants, and the unit marker trait. This crate sits at the bottom of the dependency graph. It has no dependency on any other ApsisRS crate, so every other crate may use it. Three concerns live here: - [`Error`] and [`Result`] are a general purpose error carrying a coarse [`ErrorKind`]. They exist so that a function whose failure has no interesting structure can report it without inventing a type, and so that the workspace has a shape to fall back on. They are deliberately *not* the error type of the layers: a layer with a domain specific failure defines its own `Error` and `ErrorKind`, whose variants name the concrete conditions a caller would want to match on. See `docs/design/errors.md` for why, and for the conventions the domain errors follow. - [`constant`] holds physical and astronomical constants expressed in SI units. - [`Quantity`] marks newtypes that carry a physical unit, so generic code can accept any quantity and still recover its unit type.

crates.name: apsis-units
crates.summary: Strongly typed newtypes for physical quantities. Each quantity is a newtype over `f64` that carries its unit in the type system, so a length cannot be passed where a duration is expected. Units of the same dimension convert through [`Quantity::to_unit`], and each unit also offers direct conversions for the common cases. A newtype implements both [`Unit`] and [`Quantity`], with its own type as the associated unit. For example [`Meters`] is a [`Length`](dimension::Length) unit and a quantity whose unit is itself. The dimensions covered here are length, time, frequency, angle, and thermodynamic temperature. Temperature is the only affine scale in the set, so Celsius is handled by explicit methods on [`Kelvin`] rather than by the linear [`Unit`] conversion factor. ``` use apsis_core::Quantity; use apsis_units::{Kilometers, Meters}; let distance = Meters::new(2_500.0); let in_kilometers: Kilometers = distance.to_unit(); assert!((in_kilometers.value() - 2.5).abs() < 1e-12); ```

crates.name: apsis-math
crates.summary: Dependency-free linear algebra for the ApsisRS workspace. The crate provides three types: - [`Vec3`], a three component column vector over `f64` - [`Quat`], a unit quaternion used for rotations - [`Mat3`], a three by three matrix stored in column-major order The types are plain data with no interior invariants beyond those documented on each method, so their fields are public and a value can be built by struct literal expression. Operations that are mathematically undefined for some inputs, such as normalizing the zero vector, return [`Option`] instead of panicking or producing a non-finite result. All rotations use the right-hand rule about the given axis, and all angles are in radians. Angles are not wrapped on input; methods that require a canonical range document that requirement. ``` use apsis_math::Vec3; let x = Vec3::new(1.0, 0.0, 0.0); let y = Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0); let z = x.cross(y); assert_eq!(z, Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0)); ```

crates.name: apsis-macros
crates.summary: Macros that support the ApsisRS workspace. This crate currently defines no macros. It exists so that the workspace has a single place for macro definitions if a need arises, and so that adding one later does not require a new crate. The decision to leave it empty follows from what the workspace actually needs. Rust's built in `macro_rules!` can already do everything the foundation layer requires: - Substituting a type and a literal to build a quantity, as `quantity!(Meters, 1.5)`. - Dispatching on a trailing token to accept a unit suffix, as `to_meters!(2.5 km)`. Both forms are demonstrated by the tests in `tests/probe.rs`. They can be written directly in the crate that uses them, so no shared macro crate is needed. Two limits are worth recording, because they explain why a macro based unit system is not provided: - A `macro_rules!` macro cannot be generic over a unit suffix that is not an identifier. `1.5 m` and `1.5 km` are accepted by separate rules, so the macro must enumerate every suffix it supports. The unit newtypes in `apsis-units` already give compile time unit safety without that list, so the macro would add surface area without adding checking. - A declarative macro cannot inspect the value of its arguments, so it cannot fold a unit conversion at compile time beyond what constant evaluation already does. A literal such as `2.5 * 1000.0` is folded by the compiler anyway. If the workspace later needs macros that generate items, such as deriving a set of conversions from one definition, that is the point at which this crate should gain its first macro.

crates.name: apsis-time
crates.summary: Time scales, epochs, and calendar conversions. This crate provides the time model used by the rest of the workspace. An [`Epoch`] is an instant stored as a Modified Julian Date on the International Atomic Time scale, and [`TimeScale`] names the scale a number is expressed in. Storing a single uniform scale makes the arithmetic exact: the difference between two epochs is the elapsed SI time between them, independent of the scales they were created in. UTC is not uniform, because leap seconds are inserted to keep it near the rotation of the Earth, so UTC conversions are routed through the table in `apsis-leap`. ``` use apsis_time::{Calendar, Epoch, TimeScale}; // Build an instant from a UTC calendar date and read it back. let calendar = Calendar::from_ymd(2024, 6, 15); let epoch = Epoch::from_calendar(calendar, TimeScale::Utc).expect("covered by the leap table"); let back = epoch.calendar(TimeScale::Utc).expect("covered by the leap table"); assert_eq!(back.year, 2024); assert_eq!(back.month, 6); assert_eq!(back.day, 15); ``` Sources: - Julian date and Modified Julian date conventions: IAU, as described in the *Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac*. - Terrestrial Time offset from TAI: IAU 2000 Resolution B1.9. - Leap seconds: IERS Bulletin C, embedded by `apsis-leap`. - Calendar algorithms: Howard Hinnant, *chrono-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms*, 2015.

crates.name: apsis-leap
crates.summary: Embedded leap second table for the UTC time scale. Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is kept within 0.9 s of UT1 by inserting or removing leap seconds. Because UTC is not a uniform time scale, converting between UTC and the uniform scales TAI, TT, and GPS requires the offset `TAI - UTC` in force at the instant of interest. This crate embeds that offset as a compile time table and answers queries against it. Dates are handled as Modified Julian Date (MJD), which is the Julian Date minus 2 400 000.5. An MJD is a count of days since 1858-11-17T00:00:00, so it carries no time scale of its own; the caller states the scale by choosing which function to call. The table begins at 1972-01-01, when UTC adopted the current integer second offset scheme. Offsets before that date were fractional and followed a different rule, so queries earlier than the first entry return `None` rather than a misleading value. Source: IERS Bulletin C, which announces leap seconds after confirmation by the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service. The most recent entry in this table is the leap second of 2017-01-01; no leap second has been announced since. ``` use apsis_leap::{tai_minus_utc_at_mjd, LEAP_SECONDS}; // The last entry in the embedded table fixes the current offset. let last = LEAP_SECONDS.last().expect("table is not empty"); assert_eq!(last.tai_minus_utc, 37.0); assert_eq!(tai_minus_utc_at_mjd(60_000.0), Some(37.0)); ```

The result is the MJD of 00:00:00 on the given day. The algorithm is the
Fliegel-Van Flandern integer conversion, which is exact for every date
the Gregorian calendar is defined on and does not need a lookup table.

The computation is done in `i64` and converted once at the end, so the
result is exact for the range of dates in which a leap second can

items.name: tai_minus_utc_at_mjd
items.doc:
Returns the value of `TAI - UTC` in seconds at the given UTC Modified
Julian Date.

The offset is a step function: it changes at 00:00:00 UTC on the
effective date of each leap second and is constant in between. A query
exactly on an effective date returns the new value.

Returns `None` when the instant precedes 1972-01-01, before which UTC
used fractional offsets and this table does not apply.

items.name: tai_mjd_from_utc_mjd
items.doc:
Converts a UTC Modified Julian Date to the corresponding TAI Modified
Julian Date.

The conversion adds the offset in force at that instant. Because the
offset is a step function evaluated on the UTC side, the conversion is
defined for every UTC instant; the inverse conversion is not, because a
leap second makes some TAI instants correspond to no UTC instant.

Returns `None` when the instant precedes 1972-01-01.

items.name: utc_mjd_from_tai_mjd
items.doc:
Converts a TAI Modified Julian Date to the corresponding UTC Modified
Julian Date.

Each candidate offset from the table is tried in turn. A candidate is
accepted when the offset in force at the resulting UTC instant is the
same offset that produced it. At most one offset can satisfy that
condition for a given input, so the search is unambiguous.

Returns `None` in two cases. The first is an instant before the start of
the table, where UTC carried fractional offsets that this table does not
describe. The second is an instant that falls strictly inside an
inserted leap second. Such an instant has no UTC representation, because
the UTC clock labels that interval `23:59:60`, a value that does not
exist on the continuous Modified Julian Date scale.

crates.name: apsis-coord
crates.summary: Coordinate frames and the transformations between them. This crate defines positions that carry their reference frame in the type, so a position expressed in one frame cannot be passed where another is expected. The two frames are the Earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame and the Earth-centered Earth-fixed (ECEF) frame. Three position representations are offered: - [`Eci`], an inertial Cartesian position in meters - [`Ecef`], an Earth-fixed Cartesian position in meters - [`Geodetic`], a latitude, longitude, and height above the WGS 84 ellipsoid The transformation between [`Eci`] and [`Ecef`] is the rotation defined by the Earth Rotation Angle, which `apsis-frames` computes. The transformation between [`Ecef`] and [`Geodetic`] uses the WGS 84 ellipsoid from `apsis-geodesy`. ``` use apsis_coord::{Ecef, Eci, Geodetic, WGS84}; use apsis_frames::EarthRotationAngle; use apsis_math::Vec3; // A station on the equator at zero longitude. let station = Geodetic::new(0.0, 0.0, 0.0); let fixed = station.to_ecef(); assert!((fixed.vector().x - WGS84.semi_major_axis()).abs() < 1e-6); // Rotating it into the inertial frame preserves its length. let inertial = fixed.to_eci(EarthRotationAngle::from_ut1_days(0.0)); assert!((inertial.vector().norm() - fixed.vector().norm()).abs() < 1e-6); let _ = Eci::new(Vec3::X); ``` Sources: - Earth Rotation Angle: *IERS Conventions (2010)*, equation 8.32, as implemented by `apsis-frames`. - Geodetic conversions and the WGS 84 ellipsoid: NIMA TR8350.2, third edition, 2000, as implemented by `apsis-geodesy`.

crates.name: apsis-geodesy
crates.summary: Reference ellipsoids and geodetic computations. A geodetic position is written as latitude, longitude, and height above an ellipsoid. Latitude here is always geodetic, the angle between the ellipsoid normal and the equatorial plane, not geocentric. The two differ by up to about 0.19 degrees at mid latitudes, so the distinction matters for pointing and ranging. [`WGS84`] is the ellipsoid used by GPS and by almost all satellite work. Its defining parameters are the semi-major axis and the inverse flattening; every other quantity is derived from those two, so the derived values agree with the ones published in the standard to the precision of the defining parameters. Source: National Imagery and Mapping Agency, *Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984*, Technical Report TR8350.2, third edition, 2000. ``` use apsis_geodesy::{Geodetic, WGS84}; // The equator has zero height and a radius equal to the semi-major axis. let point = Geodetic::new(0.0, 0.0, 0.0); let cartesian = point.to_cartesian(WGS84); assert!((cartesian.norm() - WGS84.semi_major_axis()).abs() < 1e-9); ```

there is no risk of the parameters disagreeing with each other.

Lengths are in meters and angles are in radians.

items.name: to_cartesian
items.signature: pub fn to_cartesian(self, ellipsoid: Ellipsoid) -> Vec3 {
items.doc:
Converts this geodetic position to Earth-fixed Cartesian coordinates
on the given ellipsoid.

The frame has its third axis along the ellipsoid's minor axis through
the north pole, its first axis through the intersection of the
equator and the prime meridian, and its second axis completing a
right-handed set. The result is in meters.

The closed form is

```text
N = a / sqrt(1 - e^2 sin^2(lat))
x = (N + h) cos(lat) cos(lon)
y = (N + h) cos(lat) sin(lon)
z = (N (1 - e^2) + h) sin(lat)
```

where `N` is the prime vertical radius of curvature. This form is
exact everywhere, including at the poles, where the cosine factors
vanish.

micrometer for positions from below the ellipsoid out to geostationary

polar axis so that no longitude is defined.

crates.name: apsis-frames
crates.summary: Reference frame definitions and the rotation between the inertial and Earth-fixed frames. A reference frame fixes the orientation and origin that a vector is expressed relative to. This crate names the two frames used for near-Earth work and computes the rotation between them. Concrete position types that carry a frame are defined in `apsis-coord`; this crate works with the rotation matrix and the angle that defines it. The inertial frame is the Earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame aligned with the mean equator and equinox of J2000.0. Its axes are fixed in inertial space, so an orbit propagated in it is not affected by the rotation of the Earth. The rotating frame is the Earth-centered Earth-fixed (ECEF) frame. Its third axis is the Earth's rotation axis and its first axis follows the prime meridian, so a point fixed to the ground has constant coordinates in it. The two are related by a rotation of [`EarthRotationAngle`] about the common third axis. This crate models the Earth's rotation with the Earth Rotation Angle, which is a function of UT1 only. It does not apply precession or nutation, because an angle accurate to a few hundredths of a degree is sufficient for pointing and coverage work and the full model needs the orientation of the celestial pole, which is a separate computation. Source: the Earth Rotation Angle expression is from the International Astronomical Union, as given in the *IERS Conventions (2010)*, equation 8.32. ``` use apsis_frames::{EarthRotationAngle, rotation_eci_to_ecef}; // The angle advances by roughly 360.9856 degrees per day. let first = EarthRotationAngle::from_ut1_days(0.0); let second = EarthRotationAngle::from_ut1_days(1.0); let advance = (second.radians() - first.radians()).to_degrees(); assert!((advance - 360.985_612_288_088).abs() < 1e-6); // The rotation is ready to apply to a vector. let _ = rotation_eci_to_ecef(first); ```

The epoch value is zero by the definition of the angle: the International

Source: IERS Conventions (2010), equation 8.32.

The value is held in turns. A turn is one full revolution, so the angle
is periodic with a period of one. The value returned is not reduced to
any interval, so differences between two angles are meaningful even when
the interval is longer than a day.

centuries from J2000.0 on the Terrestrial Time scale. The constant term

Returns the frame bias rotation matrix.

The bias is a constant rotation from the International Celestial
Reference System to the dynamical mean equator and equinox of J2000.0.
Its three angles are far below a tenth of an arcsecond, but omitting it
would leave a systematic error that is larger than the precision of the

reach the true equator and equinox of date.

radians.

The expression is a polynomial in the number of Julian centuries from
J2000.0 plus the fraction of the day in seconds of time. It is the
sidereal time the SGP4 theory was fitted against, which is why it is used
here rather than the modern expression: the element sets are consistent

fraction, because a single `f64` near 2 461 000 has a resolution of about
40 microseconds and the sidereal time is wanted to better than that. The
caller that has only one value may pass the whole part and the fraction
separately, or pass a value twice: `(jd, 0.0)`, `(2400000.5, mjd)`, and

part preserves more of the fraction.

The matrix carries a vector from the celestial reference frame to the
true equator and equinox of date. It is built from the four precession
angles with the nutation added to the last two, which is the form the
reference uses.

Returns the complementary terms of the equation of the equinoxes.

The equation of the equinoxes has, besides the projection of the nutation
in longitude onto the true equator, a set of small periodic terms from
the same theory. They reach about twice the constant term of the
osculating nutation, which is a millisecond of time, so they matter for a
sidereal time that is quoted to that precision.

Source: the MHB2000 complementary terms, as implemented by `eraEect00`.

The equation of the equinoxes is the difference between the true and mean
equinoxes measured along the true equator. It is the quantity a sidereal
time must be corrected by to become the hour angle of the true equinox.

The value is the projection of the nutation in longitude onto the true
equator, `dpsi cos(eps)`, plus the complementary terms of the theory.

The polar motion is the motion of the rotation pole within the Earth. It
is measured daily and published by the International Earth Rotation and
Reference Systems Service, so it cannot be computed from a model and is
supplied by the caller.

published values are not available.

The error from omitting the polar motion is under a tenth of an
arcsecond, well below the nutation but above the precision of a
modern transformation.

crates.name: apsis-tle
crates.summary: Parsing of two-line element sets. A two-line element set (TLE) describes a satellite orbit in the form used by the North American Aerospace Defense Command and distributed by Space-Track. The name of the satellite is carried on an optional first line, and the two following lines carry the orbital data. The format is fixed width. Every field occupies a fixed range of columns and the checksum of each line is the sum of its digits modulo ten, where a minus sign counts as one. This crate parses a TLE into structured fields and verifies the line checksums and the matching element set number. It does not interpret the fields; the mean elements and their units are the concern of `apsis-sgp4`. Column positions are one based, matching the documentation of the format. Two conventions from the format are worth stating explicitly, because they are easy to misread: - An exponent field is written as a signed single digit followed by the magnitude. For example ` 12345-3` means `0.12345e-3`, not `12345e-3`. - An assumed decimal point is written without a decimal point. For example the eccentricity field `0006703` means `0.0006703`. Source: the field layout follows the format description published by CelesTrak, *FAQs: Two-Line Element Set Format*, which documents the columns defined by the original NORAD specification. The checksum rule is the one stated there and used by Space-Track. ``` use apsis_tle::TwoLineElement; let text = concat!( "1 25544U 98067A 08264.51782528 -.00002182 00000-0 -11606-4 0 2927\r\n", "2 25544 51.6416 247.4627 0006703 130.5360 325.0288 15.72125391563537\r\n", ); let element = TwoLineElement::parse(text).expect("sample is well formed"); assert_eq!(element.satellite_number, 25544); assert!((element.eccentricity - 0.0006703).abs() < 1e-12); ```

crates.name: apsis-sgp4
crates.summary: The SGP4 and SDP4 analytical orbit propagator. The propagator takes the mean orbital elements of a two-line element set and returns the position and velocity of the satellite at a requested instant. It is the model that the element sets are fitted to, so it is the correct way to use them; a general purpose numerical integrator given the same elements would drift away from the published positions. Two branches exist and the propagator selects between them by orbital period. A satellite with a period below 225 minutes is propagated with SGP4, which models the secular effect of the Earth's oblateness and a drag term. A satellite at or above that period is propagated with SDP4, which adds the resonance and the luni-solar perturbations that dominate at that altitude. Inputs and outputs: - Elements are the mean elements from [`apsis_tle::TwoLineElement`]. Angles in the element set are in degrees and mean motion is in revolutions per day; this crate converts to radians and radians per minute internally. - The output is expressed in the True Equator Mean Equinox (TEME) frame, with position in kilometers and velocity in kilometers per second. TEME is the frame the model defines; converting it to an Earth-fixed frame requires the Earth rotation and the equation of the equinoxes and is not part of this crate. - Time is measured from the element set epoch, in minutes. Source: the algorithm follows Vallado et al., *Revisiting Spacetrack Report #3*, AIAA 2006-6753, 2006, and the revised implementation distributed with that paper. ``` use apsis_sgp4::{GravityModel, Satellite}; use apsis_tle::TwoLineElement; let text = concat!( "1 25544U 98067A 08264.51782528 -.00002182 00000-0 -11606-4 0 2927\r\n", "2 25544 51.6416 247.4627 0006703 130.5360 325.0288 15.72125391563537\r\n", ); let element = TwoLineElement::parse(text).expect("sample is well formed"); let satellite = Satellite::from_element(&element, GravityModel::WGS72) .expect("sample elements are propagatable"); // Propagate to the epoch of the elements. let state = satellite.propagate_minutes(0.0).expect("epoch state exists"); // The position of a low Earth satellite is a few thousand kilometers // from the center of the Earth. assert!(state.position.norm() > 6_600.0); assert!(state.position.norm() < 7_200.0); ```

items.name: unkozai_mean_motion
items.signature: pub fn unkozai_mean_motion( mean_motion: f64, eccentricity: f64, inclination: f64, model: GravityModel, ) -> f64 {
items.doc:
Applies the Kozai to Brouwer mean motion correction.

The mean motion in an element set is a Kozai mean motion, which the
theory must convert to a Brouwer mean motion before use. The relation is

```text
n0 = n / (1 + 1.5 k2 (3 cos^2 i - 1) / (a^2 sqrt(1 - e^2)) / a^2)
```

written in the form used here as a fixed point iteration, because `a`
depends on `n0` through Kepler's third law. The iteration converges from
the unmodified mean motion in a few steps for every orbit that appears in
an element set.
Applies the Kozai to Brouwer mean motion correction.

The mean motion in an element set is a Kozai mean motion, which the
theory must convert to a Brouwer mean motion before use. Writing `no` for
the element set value and `xke` for the Kepler constant, the reference
implementation evaluates

```text
ak   = (xke / no)^(2/3)
d1   = 0.75 j2 (3 cos^2 i - 1) / (sqrt(1 - e^2) (1 - e^2))
del  = d1 / ak^2
adel = ak (1 - del^2 - del (1/3 + 134 del^2 / 81))
del  = d1 / adel^2
n0   = no / (1 + del)
```

The second evaluation of `del` uses `adel` rather than `ak`, which is
what makes the correction consistent with the semi-major axis implied by
the corrected mean motion.

Source: Vallado et al., *Revisiting Spacetrack Report #3*, AIAA
2006-6753, 2006.

crates.name: apsis-ephemeris
crates.summary: Ephemeris sampling and interpolation. A propagator gives the state of a satellite at any instant, but calling it millions of times is wasteful when the result is only needed to draw a track or to search for a crossing. This crate records the state at a grid of times, called samples, and answers queries between them by interpolation. The two halves are deliberately independent: - [`Ephemeris`] is a table of times and states. It knows nothing about where the states came from, so a table propagated by SGP4, computed by two-body theory, or read from a file all work the same way. - [`Sampler`] fills a table by calling a function that produces a state from a time. In this workspace that function is normally `apsis_sgp4::Satellite::propagate_at`, but the sampler only requires a closure, so a test can use an analytic function. Interpolation is Hermite cubic, which uses both the position and the velocity at each end of an interval. Using the velocity is what makes it accurate: a cubic through two positions alone has no information about how fast the satellite is moving, while Hermite reconstruction matches the slope at both ends and so reproduces a smooth orbit far better for the same sample spacing. On a circular orbit the error is of order the fourth power of the step, so halving the step cuts the error about sixteen fold. Times are in seconds from an origin chosen by the caller, matching the rest of the orbit layer. Positions are in kilometers and velocities in kilometers per second. ``` use apsis_ephemeris::{Sample, Sampler}; use apsis_kepler::{GravityParameter, KeplerianElements}; // A circular orbit at the Earth's equatorial radius. let elements = KeplerianElements { semi_major_axis: 7_000.0, eccentricity: 0.0, inclination: 0.9, right_ascension: 0.0, argument_of_perigee: 0.0, true_anomaly: 0.0, }; let state_at = |seconds: f64| { let mean = 2.0 * core::f64::consts::PI * seconds / elements.period(GravityParameter::WGS84); let state = elements .with_mean_anomaly(mean) .to_state(GravityParameter::WGS84) .expect("the orbit is valid"); Sample::new(seconds, state.position, state.velocity) }; let sampler = Sampler::new(0.0, 600.0, 60.0); let ephemeris = sampler.sample(state_at).expect("the grid is usable"); assert_eq!(ephemeris.len(), 11); // A query between two samples is interpolated. let state = ephemeris.state_at(30.0).expect("the time is covered"); assert!(state.position.norm() > 6_900.0); ```

crates.name: apsis-maneuver
crates.summary: Impulsive and finite orbital maneuver models. A maneuver changes an orbit by applying thrust. The two models here are the two ends of the spectrum. An impulsive maneuver, [`Impulse`], applies a velocity change instantaneously, so the position is unchanged and only the velocity jumps. This is the model for a chemical burn, whose duration is short compared with the orbital period, and it is the model every textbook delta-v budget is written in. It is exact in the limit of zero burn time and the source of the closed form results for transfers between two orbits. A finite maneuver, [`FiniteBurn`], applies a constant acceleration over a duration, so the position drifts during the burn and the achieved velocity change is less than the thrust would give in free space when the thrust has to fight gravity. It is the model for an electric thruster, whose burn may last a large fraction of an orbit, and for any burn where the short duration approximation is not good enough. The two agree in the limit: a finite burn of acceleration `a` over a duration `t` delivers the impulse `a t`, so a [`FiniteBurn`] with a vanishing duration converges on the matching [`Impulse`]. The tests check that limit, which is what ties the two models together. The impulsive model also provides the classic two impulse transfer between two coplanar circular orbits, [`hohmann_transfer`], which is the reference every low thrust result is compared against. It gives the two burns and the total delta-v for a transfer between two circular orbits of given radii, together with the transfer time, the half period of the transfer ellipse. Conventions match the rest of the orbit layer: lengths are in kilometers, velocities in kilometers per second, and angles in radians. ``` use apsis_maneuver::{Impulse, hohmann_transfer}; use apsis_kepler::GravityParameter; use apsis_math::Vec3; // An impulsive burn straight along the velocity. let impulse = Impulse::new(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)).expect("the change is usable"); assert!((impulse.magnitude() - 1.0).abs() < 1e-12); // The two burns that raise a circular orbit from 7000 to 8000 km. let transfer = hohmann_transfer(7_000.0, 8_000.0, GravityParameter::WGS84) .expect("the radii are usable"); assert!(transfer.first_burn > 0.0); assert!(transfer.total_delta_v() > 0.0); ```

A finite burn is the model for a thruster that is on for long enough that

appreciably while thrusting.

The acceleration is held constant in an inertial frame chosen by the
caller. That is the simplification this model makes: a real thruster
fires along a body axis that rotates as the spacecraft turns to hold a
direction, and modelling that requires the attitude history, which is not
part of this crate.

gravity changes the velocity during the burn even with no thrust, so

coast isolates the contribution of the thrust, which is what the
burn bought; it also makes the result converge on the nominal change
as the duration shrinks, which the difference from the initial
velocity would not.

velocity change.

The transfer is the classic Hohmann maneuver: a burn onto an ellipse
whose perigee touches the lower orbit and whose apogee touches the upper

destination circle. It is the cheapest two impulse transfer between two
coplanar circular orbits in the impulsive model, which is why it is the
reference every other transfer is measured against.

raises the orbit and a negative one lowers it, so the same type covers a
climb and a descent. The total is the sum of the magnitudes, which is the
quantity a propellant budget uses.

items.name: hohmann_transfer
items.signature: pub fn hohmann_transfer( from_radius: f64, to_radius: f64, parameter: GravityParameter, ) -> Result<HohmannTransfer, ManeuverError> {
items.doc:
Returns the two impulse transfer between two circular orbits.

The radii are in kilometers and must be finite and positive. The two may
be given in either order: a larger second radius is a climb and a smaller
one a descent.

Returns an error when a radius is not usable or when the two are equal,
because a transfer between an orbit and itself is not a maneuver and is
almost always a mistake in a plan.

The burns follow from the vis-viva equation. At the first radius the
circular speed is `sqrt(mu / r1)` and the speed on the transfer ellipse
is `sqrt(mu (2 / r1 - 1 / a))`, where `a` is the semi-major axis of the
ellipse, so the first burn is the difference. The second burn is the
difference between the circular speed at the destination and the speed on
the ellipse there, taken the other way round because the ellipse arrives
slower than the circle it must join. The coast time is half the period of
the ellipse.

items.name: Impulse
items.doc:
An instantaneous change in velocity.

An impulse is a velocity change applied in zero time, so it changes the
velocity of a state but not its position. That is the model for a burn
short compared with the orbital period, and it is how a delta-v budget is
written.

The change is stored as a vector in the same frame as the state it will
be applied to, so the caller is responsible for expressing it in that
frame. The magnitude is the delta-v, the quantity a propellant budget is
measured in.

crates.name: apsis-orbit
crates.summary: Orbital state facade that integrates the orbit layer. This crate is the single entry point to the orbit layer. It re-exports the element parsing, the analytical propagator, and the two-body model, and adds one type that ties them together. [`Orbit`] holds a satellite prepared for propagation together with the gravity model it was initialised against, and offers the conversions between the two ways of describing an orbit that the layer supports: - Mean elements propagated by SGP4, which is the model a two-line element set is written for and the only way to reproduce the published positions of a catalogued satellite. - Instantaneous Keplerian elements, which describe the osculating two-body orbit at one instant and are useful for inspection and for planning a maneuver. The two descriptions are not interchangeable. Propagating mean elements with the two-body model, or osculating elements with SGP4, gives a different and wrong answer; the conversions here are explicit about which direction they go. Two further operations are built on the propagation and exposed here because they need the same gravity parameter to stay consistent: - [`Orbit::sample_ephemeris`] records the track on a time grid so that it can be queried by interpolation instead of by propagation, which is what a coverage or access search wants. - [`Orbit::apply_burn`] applies a finite maneuver to the osculating state and returns the resulting elements, which is what a maneuver plan produces. ``` use apsis_orbit::{GravityModel, Orbit}; use apsis_tle::TwoLineElement; let text = concat!( "1 25544U 98067A 08264.51782528 -.00002182 00000-0 -11606-4 0 2927\r\n", "2 25544 51.6416 247.4627 0006703 130.5360 325.0288 15.72125391563537\r\n", ); let element = TwoLineElement::parse(text).expect("sample is well formed"); let orbit = Orbit::from_element(&element, GravityModel::WGS72) .expect("sample elements are propagatable"); let state = orbit.propagate_minutes(60.0).expect("state exists"); assert!(state.speed() > 7.0); // The osculating elements at that instant. let osculating = orbit.osculating_elements(60.0).expect("state exists"); assert!(osculating.eccentricity < 0.01); ```

items.doc:
Returns the osculating Keplerian elements at a number of minutes from
the element epoch.

The osculating elements describe the two-body orbit that matches the
position and velocity at that instant. They are not the mean elements
of the element set, and they change along the orbit because SGP4
includes perturbations that the two-body model does not.

Returns an error when the state cannot be propagated, or when the
instantaneous orbit is not elliptical, which can happen for a state
the propagation has pushed onto an escape trajectory.

items.name: sample_ephemeris
items.signature: pub fn sample_ephemeris( &self, start_minutes: f64, end_minutes: f64, step_minutes: f64, ) -> Result<apsis_ephemeris::Ephemeris, EphemerisSamplingError> {
items.doc:
Samples the orbit into an ephemeris over a range of minutes.

The propagation is the expensive part of a track, so a table built
once and queried many times is worth the memory. The sample times are
minutes from the element epoch, matching the rest of this type, while
the returned ephemeris keeps seconds, matching `apsis-ephemeris`.

The table is built with position and velocity from the propagator,
so the Hermite interpolation has exact endpoint slopes and the error
between samples is tiny; there is no need to use the position only
route except for a source that has no velocity.

Returns an error when the grid is not usable or when a sample cannot
be propagated, which happens when the elements have decayed or the
range leaves the region where the model is defined.

items.name: apply_burn
items.signature: pub fn apply_burn( &self, minutes: f64, burn: apsis_maneuver::FiniteBurn, steps: usize, ) -> Result<KeplerianElements, ManeuverApplicationError> {
items.doc:
Applies a finite burn and returns the resulting osculating elements.

The burn is applied to the osculating state at the given time, so the
manoeuvre is described relative to the orbit the satellite is
actually on rather than the mean elements. The resulting elements are
the osculating elements of the post burn state, which is what a
following propagation needs. Because the underlying propagator is
built for one element set, this is a planning result rather than a
new propagator; a caller that wants to propagate the new orbit starts
a fresh `Orbit` from the returned elements.
